title: A bowl of stew (Genesis 25:27–34)
hookLine: Esau, starving, trades his birthright for lentils
carry: not for a bowl of stew

lines: TWINS: RED ESAU, JACOB AT HIS HEEL.
cards: Eleven at night, nothing in the fridge, and a gas-station burrito looks like the best idea anyone ever had. Hunger shrinks the future: what's on the plate outweighs anything promised for next month.

Rebekah, the girl from the well, has twins now, and they fought before they were born. Esau came out first, red and hairy; Jacob came second, holding his brother's heel. Esau grows up a hunter, his father's favorite.
Jacob is a quiet man who stays among the tents, his mother's favorite. One day Esau comes in from the field, empty-handed and exhausted, and smells something cooking.

teach.b: Esau says, in the King James Bible: "Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint."
The Hebrew is blunter, something like let me gulp down some of that red stuff, and the text adds that's why he was called Edom, which means red.

Jacob names a price: sell me this day thy birthright. The birthright belonged to the firstborn son: a larger share of the inheritance, a double share under later law, and the place of head of the family.
The future, packed into one word.

teach.h: WHAT PROFIT SHALL IT DO TO ME?
teach.b: Esau answers: "Behold, I am at the point to die: and what profit shall this birthright do to me?" He's hungry, not dying, but hunger feels like dying. Jacob makes him swear, then gives him bread and lentil stew.
Four verbs, flat as a ledger: he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way.

And the verdict: "thus Esau despised his birthright." The story doesn't call Jacob a hero; he takes advantage of his hungry brother. And it doesn't call Esau a victim; he treated the future as worth one meal.
The letter to the Hebrews later uses Esau as a warning: he sold his birthright for one morsel of meat. The old phrase a mess of pottage isn't actually in the King James text.
It comes from chapter headings in older English Bibles. But the picture stuck: something lasting, traded for a bowl.

how: Christians often read Esau's choice as a warning about trading lasting things for quick ones, and Hebrews 12:16 is preached in many churches alongside teaching on patience and self-control.

games.q: you're Esau, home from the field, exhausted. your brother says: sell me your birthright for this bowl of stew. what do you do?
o: laugh, and make yourself some bread.
say: I'm about to die, what good is a birthright? and swear.
ask your mother to settle it.
games.why: "what profit shall this birthright do to me?" he swears, eats, drinks, rises, and goes his way. "thus Esau despised his birthright."

practice: Where are you most likely to trade the long thing for the quick one: sleep for one more episode, a friendship for a cutting remark, savings for a purchase you'll forget, your word for an easy excuse?
Picture that moment, the hunger and the smell of stew, and yourself pausing for one breath to ask: what am I trading? If you pray, you can ask for patience.

wordCard.voice: Birthright. The firstborn's inheritance and place in the family, the future in one word, which Esau trades for a bowl of red lentil stew.

orig.note: Hebrew: birthright, the right of the firstborn.
